newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav political risks deter foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav political risks deter foreign investors.

text.p: Yugoslavia is deterring foreign investors by an unwillingness to meet international political and economic conditions, experts said.

They warned the risks are still too high and the country remains just a "potential" target for future investment and trade opportunities despite large international community interest to do business here.

"The risks are still too high. If you make political and economic risk assesment it comes out hold. Exploratory and hold. Wait and see what the future brings," said one U.S. investor, who asked not to be named.
The central geographic location of Serbia and Montenegro, the two units of the new Yugoslav federation, in the Balkans are attractive for foreign investors.
But experts say they also have highly educated people, a good workforce, relatively good industrial and energy base and a lot of experience in doing business with the West.

Once a market-oriented bastion of relative wealth amid struggling, impoverished communist economies, the country reels today from the violent break-up of the former federation, loss of markets, mismanagement and the impact of a four-year U.N. trade embargo.
Experts reckon the country will need some two billion dollars a year by the year 2000 if it is to avoid an economic abyss.

Foreign capital is seen as the only way to resuscitate the economy. Annual per capita income is down to $1,500 or half its pre-war 1990 level, most of its population is below the poverty line, corruption and the black market are booming, and production has collapsed.
Expectations for fresh foreign funds fell short following the lifting of the U.S. trade embargo last October, as the United States kept a so-called outer wall of sanctions.

Removal of this outer wall is linked to the political conditions forcing Belgrade to respect human rights in mostly-Albanian southern province of Kosovo, cooperate with the Hague War Crimes Tribunal, speed up talks on division of assets of the old federation, and widen democracy.

Experts agreed the interest for business is obvious, but the political framework and lack of agreements with the International Monetary Fund and other international organisations are still an obstacle to normalisation of trade and investment flows.

"Both political and economic risks are too great until the outer wall of sanctions is removed." another U.S. businessman said. "Political atmosphere is the key factor. Investors do not like to go into a country where the political future is uncertain and potentially unstable."

Analysts also said a free and open economy, rid of the influence of communist-era management, and implementation of a serious privatisation programme would help a lot in attracting foreign capital inflow.
Businessmen agreed everything is up to the Yugoslav government as it must create favourable conditions if it wants to see foreign investors flock here.
